steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Geometric problems need geometric solutions, like the ones developed under the umbrella of geometric deep learning. The main design principle of this field is equivariance to symmetry groups, which means that network outputs should transform consistently when the inputs undergo symmetry transformations. This idea has led to architectures that were successfully used for problems from molecular modelling to robotics.

At the same time as modern geometric deep learning developed, the transformer became the de-facto standard architecture in a wide range of domains. Transformers are expressive and versatile, and their training dynamics are stable. Most importantly, they scale well to large systems, which is mostly because pairwise interactions are computed through a plain dot product and because highly optimized implementations exist.

These two threads have only recently been combined. Different equivariant transformer architectures have been proposed, but most of them involve expensive pairwise interactions, which either require restricted receptive fields or limit the scalability to large systems. Recent work introduced the Geometric Algebra Transformer (GATr), which to the best of our knowledge is the first equivariant transformer architecture that is based purely on dot-product attention. The key idea that makes this possible is representing data in the projective geometric algebra. This algebra supports embedding various kinds of 3D data and it has an expressive invariant inner product.

- This paper
  - generalize GATr to arbitrary geometric (Clifford) algebras; scalable equivariant transformer for any of them
  - Euclidean and conformal besides projective; all three represent 3D data
- Comparison
  - theory: expressivity, 3D positions, attention from Euclidean distances
  - experiments: n -body modelling, wall shear stress on large artery meshes
  - normalization, training stability
- Findings
  - all viable, unique strengths
  - Euclidean simplest, most memory-efficient; smaller symmetry group, less sample-efficient
  - projective: simplest form not expressive enough; improved version good
  - conformal: harder normalization; elegant 3D geometry, strong results

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Geometric problems need geometric solutions, like the ones developed under the umbrella of geometric deep learning. The main design principle of this field is equivariance to symmetry groups, which means that network outputs should transform consistently when the inputs undergo symmetry transformations. This idea has led to architectures that were successfully used for problems from molecular modelling to robotics.

At the same time as modern geometric deep learning developed, the transformer became the de-facto standard architecture in a wide range of domains. Transformers are expressive and versatile, and their training dynamics are stable. Most importantly, they scale well to large systems, which is mostly because pairwise interactions are computed through a plain dot product and because highly optimized implementations exist.

These two threads have only recently been combined. Different equivariant transformer architectures have been proposed, but most of them involve expensive pairwise interactions, which either require restricted receptive fields or limit the scalability to large systems. Recent work introduced the Geometric Algebra Transformer (GATr), which to the best of our knowledge is the first equivariant transformer architecture that is based purely on dot-product attention. The key idea that makes this possible is representing data in the projective geometric algebra. This algebra supports embedding various kinds of 3D data and it has an expressive invariant inner product.

In this paper, we generalize the GATr architecture to arbitrary geometric (or Clifford) algebras. We show how to construct a scalable, equivariant transformer architecture for any such algebra. Besides the projective algebra that was used by the original GATr work, we focus on the Euclidean and conformal geometric algebra, and we discuss how all three of them can represent 3D data.

We compare GATr variations based on these three algebras. In theory, we study their expressivity, how they represent 3D positions, and whether they can compute attention based on Euclidean distances. In experiments, we compare the architectures on n -body modelling tasks and on predicting wall shear stress on large artery meshes. We also comment on issues with normalization and training stability.

All variations of the GATr architecure turn out to be viable, and each has unique strengths. The Euclidean architecture is the simplest and the most memory-efficient, but its symmetry group is smaller and it is less sample-efficient. The projective algebra in its simplest form is not expressive enough, but an improved, more complex version performs well. The conformal algebra makes normalization more challenging, but it gives an elegant formulation of 3D geometry and strong experimental results.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Geometric problems require geometric solutions, such as those developed under the umbrella of geometric deep learning [1]. The primary design principle of this field is equivariance to symmetry groups [2]: network outputs should transform consistently under symmetry transformations of the inputs. This idea has sparked architectures that have been successfully deployed on problems ranging from molecular modelling to robotics.

In parallel to the development of modern geometric deep learning, the transformer [3] has become the de-facto standard architecture across a wide range of domains. Transformers are expressive, versatile, and exhibit stable training dynamics. Crucially, they scale well to large systems, mostly thanks to computing pairwise interactions through a plain dot product and to the existence of highly optimized implementations [4,5].

Only recently have these two threads been brought together. While different equivariant transformer architectures have been proposed [6,7,8], most involve expensive pairwise interactions that either require restricted receptive fields or limit scalability to large systems. [9] introduced the Geometric Algebra Transformer (GATr), to the best of our knowledge the first equivariant transformer architecture based purely on dot-product attention. The key enabling idea is to represent data in the projective geometric algebra, which supports the embedding of various kinds of 3D data and has an expressive invariant inner product.

In this paper, we generalize the GATr architecture to arbitrary geometric (or Clifford) algebras, and show how to construct a scalable, equivariant transformer architecture for any such algebra. In addition to the projective algebra used by [9], we focus on the Euclidean and conformal geometric algebra, and discuss how all three can represent 3D data.

We compare GATr variations based on these three algebras. Theoretically, we study their expressivity, their representation of 3D positions, and their ability to compute attention based on Euclidean distances. Experimentally, we compare the architectures on n -body modelling tasks and on the prediction of wall shear stress on large artery meshes. We also comment on normalization and training stability issues.

All variations of the GATr architecure prove viable, each with unique strengths. The Euclidean architecture is the simplest and most memory-efficient, but it has a smaller symmetry group and is less sample-efficient. The projective algebra is not expressive enough in its simplest form, but performs well in an improved, more complex version. The conformal algebra makes normalization more challenging, but offers an elegant formulation of 3D geometry and strong experimental results.
